body.text: APEC has long advanced and promoted an agenda that centered on open trade, connectivity and growth, and technological and knowledge exchanges, which has been largely successful. However, the geopolitical and geoeconomic events of the last years have put in doubt the underlying basis for this growth: namely, that supply chains will function without significant interruption and that goods, energy and inputs will keep flowing.

Supply chains that run through the Strait of Hormuz remain highly disrupted. Economic protection measures are increasing across the APEC region, influencing the flow of goods, but also increasingly the flow of capital and ideas. Furthermore, the acceleration of AI development and the green transition are creating a competition for much needed resources, from semiconductor chips to batteries and everything needed for the production of materials involved in both technological advancements.

Finally, we are witnessing the impact of environmental crises. In Vietnam alone, Typhoon Yagi in 2024, the power shortages of 2023, and the storms and floods of 2025 each caused losses amounting to the hundreds of millions or billions of U.S. dollars. Across Asia environmental crises are increasing and putting a further strain on the interconnectivity throughout the APEC region.

While these events differ in origin – geopolitical, geoeconomic, and climatic – they each cause disruptions to the flows on which lean supply chains depend. That, in turn, affects the ability of APEC nations to successfully cooperate, now and in the future, and to advance successful economic integration and growth.

This raises questions about whether, and to what extent, open trade and connectivity can keep functioning as engines for growth and cooperation. Given these conditions, APEC should adapt and take into consideration how resilience should be incorporated into its cooperative framework.

For the last four decades, manufacturing across the APEC region relied on “just-in-time” production, which minimizes inventory and assumes uninterrupted supply. This worked as long as geopolitical and geoeconomic disruptions were minimal. However, given present conditions the just-in-time model easily translates into “just too late.” Lean inventories give commercial actors a time-to-survive of days; restoring affected supply chains by opening a strait, repairing a port affected by a storm, or getting the required an export license takes weeks or months.

While shorter disruptions of less than three months can be absorbed through hedging, increased inventory, and temporary cost absorption, disruptions lasting significantly longer – as we are currently observing across multiple supply chains – fundamentally change the economic calculus. The answer to this is to increase resilience across APEC networks. Three priorities stand out: 1) shared buffer capacity for energy, fertilizer, food, and industrial inputs; 2) port overflow arrangements agreed in advance, since cargo rarely shifts to alternative ports without prior planning; and 3) shared early-warning services that combine data on traffic, prices, weather, and salinity for public and private users. The sum of these would increase the agility of supply chain networks across the APEC region and the ability to withstand shocks – ensuring that further economic cooperation across the APEC region remains possible.

What does this shift mean for Vietnam, an economy that has tied itself more closely to these networks than almost any other in the region? Vietnam’s integration into regional production and trade networks has been remarkable. Electronics, Vietnam’s primary export product, earned $164 billion in 2025. Within that group, exports of computers, electronic products, and components alone rose 48.4 percent to $107.7 billion. Vietnam’s total exports reached $215.7 billion in the first five months of 2026, while port throughput rose by 15 percent and container throughput by 14 percent over the same period.

These figures illustrate how Vietnam has become an integral part of the APEC value chains, which has also had a net positive impact on Vietnam’s own economic development. By linking itself economically with APEC partners and integrating itself into these networks, Vietnam has been able to gain significant economic benefits and advantages.

At the same time, despite Vietnam’s progress there is room for it to increase its position in the value chain. Questions remain on what the best means are. Education as a means to increase innovation and research is necessary and could lead to pathways to higher value-added activities. However, we equally need to observe that across the APEC region, education, innovation, and research will continue to be further advanced. In this regard Vietnam has to not only improve its own systems, but simultaneously ensure that it bridges the existing gap it has vis-à-vis other nations.

Vietnam’s position in regional networks could enable it to achieve further advancement in regional value chains. As a result of the aforementioned geopolitical, geoeconomic, and environmental issues, supply chains are moving from “just-in-time” to “just-in-case.” This offers Vietnam a good opportunity for higher value-added activity as these supply chain reconfigurations work in its favor.

First, firms pursuing “China+1” strategies regard Vietnam as the most credible Southeast Asian alternative for high-value manufacturing, on the condition that it is able to provide policy responses that are timely, meet the demands of these reconfigured supply chains, and most importantly are adequate relative to its neighbors.

The energy transition, both in the green domain and equally in fossil fuels, offers a second opening. In the wake of the Strait of Hormuz supply chain vulnerabilities, we can expect a long-term effort to reduce dependency on Gulf region energy sources. The success of China in terms of managing its energy security is an evident blueprint for how to manage this successfully. Reducing this dependence requires LNG terminals, solar and wind capacity, grid management, and energy efficiency and it is in these areas that Vietnam is ahead of many regional peers.

In this regard, resilience itself can become a key variable that Vietnam can provide to the region. It can do so as a stable actor that has reliable supply chains, with the necessary means and the ability to withstand shocks and keep functioning. Vietnam has four advantages for this role: a coastline on the main Malacca-to-Northeast-Asia shipping corridor, a food and manufacturing base, expanding ports, and a non-aligned foreign policy.

In terms of non-alignment, as strategic competition intensifies, the question of well-functioning supply chains effectively becomes a question of trust. Who controls the storage? Who gains access in a crisis? On what terms? Would a user in one bloc rely on reserves held inside another? In this regard a neutral host would play an important role in supply chain networks.

A “neutral host” should function as a storage location that every user can expect to access on equal terms in a crisis, because the host belongs to no military bloc, nor has a clear political alliance with a favored nation. Losing a reputation for neutrality – or never acquiring it – can leave the perception among other actors that storage inside one bloc is a new chokepoint, along the lines of Farrell and Newman’s “weaponized interdependence” concept.

Here Vietnam already has a starting advantage. Its “Four Nos” defense policy and its 15 comprehensive strategic partnerships, which include all five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, give it a regional leading position as a neutral actor in supply chains.

Observing the regional competitors, it is evident that Vietnam leads. The Philippines and Thailand are U.S. treaty allies. While Indonesia and Malaysia are also non-aligned, and Indonesia has offered to host a regional oil storage hub, Vietnam can make the case that it can function as a neutral and reliable actor in terms of supply chain base, in combination with a growing agricultural and manufacturing base and expanding ports.

The sum of this enables Vietnam to possibly function as an actor within APEC-focused supply chains that can offer more than its neighbors. It can function as a host for energy (of various forms), while equally supplying fertilizer storage and developing a buffer of agricultural products, such as rice and industrial inputs. Achieving such a position would give Vietnam the kind of functional niche that allows it to maximize its middle-power status beyond its material size.

Geography and neutrality are, however, only the starting point. To achieve this and to translate opportunities into actual reality, Vietnam will need to attract high-quality investment, which will be, above all, an institutional task. While a storage depot can be built in 24–30 months, it requires mechanisms for investment and operations that have yet to be resolved. In this regard, there is a necessity to match economic situations, and opportunities for that matter, with an aligned political and governance reality.

Possible development could proceed along the following sequence over two to three years. First, develop enterprise investment with state-paid storage fees, and enable lease models for regional clients with a bonded storage regime. Second, reserve depots, harvest-time rice storage, and new berths could follow in the second year, and, finally, once the infrastructure is established, the necessary policy frameworks should be implemented that allow for establishing regional buffer services linked to ASEAN and bilateral arrangements.

The areas in which Vietnam should focus to achieve the greatest potential for cooperation align with the region’s broader supply chain necessities. First, it should establish strategic reserves for energy, building on Politburo Resolution 70, which targets petroleum reserves equal to about 90 days of net imports by 2030. Vietnam should extend these efforts to include liquefied natural gas, fertilizer, rice, medical supplies, and critical industrial inputs.

Second, it should develop bonded, multi-commodity storage in port zones, open to regional actors. Third, and in tandem, it should establish port overflow arrangements agreed in advance, for instance with Singapore and Port Klang.

Fourth, and taking into consideration how environmental crises have affected food security, it should invest in harvest-time rice storage, as the Vietnam Food Association has proposed, to protect farm incomes when prices swing.

Fifth, it should seek to further advance its energy transition and cooperation in LNG, solar and wind, grid management and energy efficiency. This could be achieved through APEC partners, but also beyond, with partners such as Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands.

Overall, it becomes evident that in these times of supply chain interruption and crisis, Vietnam has a favored geography, much-needed partnerships and political neutrality, and the necessary production base to develop itself into a resilient and reliable essential actor in the just-in-case supply chain model that is gaining in importance and utility. Now Vietnam needs to build the institutions that turn these into capacity others can trust.
